text:
Artificial intelligence is often presented as a tool that can expand access to high-quality education. AI tutors, translation services, and digital learning platforms may support students who previously lacked specialised assistance. However, unequal access to technology means that AI may also deepen existing educational divisions.

Students with reliable internet connections, modern devices, and paid AI subscriptions can benefit from continuous academic support. They may receive detailed explanations, writing feedback, language assistance, and personalised study plans outside normal school hours. Students without these resources may depend entirely on limited classroom support. As a result, differences in digital access can produce differences in learning opportunities.

The quality of AI use also depends on digital literacy. Students who understand how to ask precise questions, verify outputs, and apply feedback thoughtfully are likely to gain more value than those who accept AI responses without evaluation. Wealthier schools may provide structured training and supervised access, while under-resourced institutions may lack both technical infrastructure and qualified staff.

Bias presents another concern. AI systems are trained on large collections of existing data, which may contain cultural, linguistic, or social imbalances. Students from less represented backgrounds may receive examples or explanations that do not reflect their experiences. Automated evaluation systems may also disadvantage writing styles or language patterns that differ from dominant academic norms.

AI can reduce educational inequality only when access, training, and system design are addressed together. Providing software alone is insufficient. Governments and institutions must invest in infrastructure, teacher preparation, inclusive datasets, and digital literacy. Without such measures, AI may benefit students who are already advantaged while leaving others further behind.
